old: Its second half once described running or a course, borrowed for a track built for horses long before it meant a runway for machines.
It first named a flying machine itself, coined in 1897, before settling on the meaning of an airfield.
It shares its ending with hippodrome, both built from a Greek word for a course or race.
clues: This old-fashioned name for a kind of transport site was first given by inventor Samuel Langley in 1897 to his flying machine itself, not to any place.
Today it means a field where aircraft take off and land, a quainter, more old-fashioned word than airport and often used for smaller, simpler airfields.
Its ending was shaped by analogy with hippodrome, the Greek-derived word for a horse racecourse, as if the racetrack had been reimagined for planes.
